title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
In this analysis, I look at Median Gross Rent across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

my_state <- "NY"       
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     


county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

county_data <- county_data %>%

Hamilton County, New York, a rural county Northwest of Albany, has the highest margin of error relative to its estimate. Hamilton County has an 11% margin of error when calculating estimated Median Gross Rent.

51 counties in New York fall into the high confidence category, 10 in the moderate confidence category, and 1 in the low confidence category.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York        1252     22  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York       754     33   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York         1436     11 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York         914     26  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York    759     30   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York         895     39   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))


county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        381479.
2 Moderate                11         37898.


With the increased moderate confidence moe_pct threshold from moe_pct < 10 to moe_pct < 15, there are no longer any counties that fall in the low confidence category and instead, counties that fall in the moderate confidence category increase from 10 to 11.
Counties that fall in the high confidence category have an average population of 381,479 while counties that fall in the moderate confidence category have an average population of 37,898. The median population of 381,479 is nearly 10x the population size of the moderate confidence counties (37,898).
We have the least confident data for smaller, more rural counties. The four least populous counties fall within the moderate confidence category. The remaining 7 counties that fall in the moderate confidence category all fall within the bottom 39th percentile of least populous counties in the state. One reason this could be the case, is that smaller samples provide less confidence given higher rates of variability. Additionally, sparsely populated counties, like Hamilton County (11% moe) and Schuyler County (8.7% moe), require significantly more work for those gathering data. In denser more populous counties like Queens, Kings, and Bronx counties, (all with less than 1% moe), data gathering requires much less travel. Given the higher rate of variability in smaller sample sizes, those in rural, less populous and sparsely populated areas may be inequitably represented by the data. Varying confidence rates allow policy makers to take into account data imprecision. Policy makers or state agencies should not treat data from counties with such divergent population sizes as comparable.

title: Verify the Claim: Before the world changed: New census data looks at pre-Covid San Francisco
text:
In 2022, the SF Standard, a San Francisco news outlet, published an article entitled, “Before the world changed: New census data looks at pre-Covid San Francisco: The latest ACS five-year study gives robust information on the city’s neighborhoods.” It was comprised of a number of various maps and accompanying reports documenting how San Francisco’s demographics shifted between the recently released 5-year American Community Survey (2016-2020) and the prior most recent non overlapping survey (2011-2015). The first map highlights the percent change of average household income in each San Francisco zipcode between the two 5-year ACS reports. It does not mention its methodology or approach to analyzing the data. I am interested in knowing if it was incorporated or addressed in the calculation of the percent change.
The article does not explicitly say what variable it is using to calculate the average household income per zipcode, so to be sure I was on the right track, I pulled both the median household income as well as the mean household income (DP03_0063E). Comparing the two forms of averages, it was evident that the article used mean. The mean household income data accounts for inflation, calculated based on the year the report is issued. Additionally, median household income is top-coded in 5-year ACS tract level data, meaning that there is a cap on the highest income to protect privacy. While it may not impact the true median, it is a notable decision from the Census Bureau.
The two ACS reports do not overlap.


Show code
library(tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)

sf_tract_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = "DP03_0063E",
  state = "CA",
  county = "San Francisco",
  year = 2020,
  survey = "acs5"
)

  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

sf_tract_income <- sf_tract_income %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
    ))

  aes(x=estimate, y = moe_pct)+
  geom_point()

Because I am not calculating a rate from two separate counts, and because mean is an aggregate of data, not a count, moe_prop() does not apply here.
The NA data is located in tracts that are primarily parkland, pacific ocean, or bay. I decided to keep them in, because they all have some level of data in one of the ACS reports.

  get_mean_hh_income_sf <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = "DP03_0063E",
    county = "San Francisco",
    state     = "CA",
    year      = yr,
    survey    = "acs5"
  ) %>%
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr))
}

mean_hh_income_sf_change <- bind_rows(
  get_mean_hh_income_sf(2015),
  get_mean_hh_income_sf(2020)
)

mean_hh_income_sf_new <- mean_hh_income_sf_change %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, estimate, moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(estimate, moe)
  )

hh_income_tested <- mean_hh_income_sf_new %>%
  mutate(
    change   = `estimate_2016-2020` - `estimate_2011-2015`,
    se_1     = `moe_2011-2015` / 1.645,
    se_2     = `moe_2016-2020` / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )
  
hh_income_tested %>%
  count(significant)

title: Verify the Claim: Before the world changed: New census data looks at pre-Covid San Francisco
text:
In 2022, the SF Standard, a San Francisco news outlet, published an article entitled, “Before the world changed: New census data looks at pre-Covid San Francisco: The latest ACS five-year study gives robust information on the city’s neighborhoods.” It was comprised of a number of various maps and accompanying reports documenting how San Francisco’s demographics shifted between the recently released 5-year American Community Survey (2016-2020) and the prior most recent non overlapping survey (2011-2015). The first map highlights the percent change of average household income in each San Francisco zipcode between the two 5-year ACS reports. It does not mention its methodology or approach to analyzing the data. I am interested in knowing if it was incorporated or addressed in the calculation of the percent change.
The article does not explicitly say what variable it is using to calculate the average household income per zipcode, so to be sure I was on the right track, I pulled both the median household income as well as the mean household income (DP03_0063E). Comparing the two forms of averages, it was evident that the article used mean. The mean household income data accounts for inflation, calculated based on the year the report is issued. Additionally, median household income is top-coded in 5-year ACS tract level data, meaning that there is a cap on the highest income to protect privacy. While it may not impact the true median, it is a notable decision from the Census Bureau.
The two ACS reports do not overlap.


Show code
sf_tract_income %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, "San Francisco County, California")) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, "Census")) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, moe), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "maroon") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      family = "sans",
      face = "bold",
      size = 12,
      color = "black",
      hjust = 0,
      vjust = 0,
      )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "SF Mean Household Income Estimates by Largest Marging of Error",
    subtitle = "San Francisco Census Tracts, ACS 2020 5-year estimates",
    x = "Tract",
    y = "Mean Household Income and MOE"
    )









This graph illustrates the notably high MOE for certain tracts. Upon further review, the tracts with the highest rate of margin of error are in areas with low resident density.
Because I am not calculating a rate from two separate counts, and because mean is an aggregate of data, not a count, moe_prop() does not apply here.
The NA data is located in tracts that are primarily parkland, pacific ocean, or bay. I decided to keep them in, because they all have some level of data in one of the ACS reports.


Show code
reliability_table <- sf_tract_income %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100,
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, " San Francisco County, California")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  select(dot, NAME, estimate, moe, cv, flag)

reliability_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, moe), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = cv, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot      = "",
    NAME     = "Tract",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    moe      = "MOE",
    cv       = "CV (%)",
    flag     = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%
  tab_header(
    title    = "Mean Household Income by San Francisco Census Tract",
    subtitle = "San Francisco Census Tracts, ACS 2020 5-year estimates"
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    "Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable."
  )

The article’s broadest claim is that each Zip code in San Francisco saw an increase in mean household income between the ACS15 and ACS20. Based on my analysis, it does not seem as if the article took the margin of error into account when providing estimates of rate of income increase. Of the 155 tracts with estimates in both periods, 117 show an increase in mean household income that is statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence, while 38 show changes that fall within their margins of error.
Several claims cannot be determined from this analysis. The specific percentage gains, over 75% in 94158 and 94102 and over 50% in 94118, 94131, and 94123, are reported for ZIP codes, while my analysis used tracts.
Rewrite:
In the late 2010s, household incomes rose in much of San Francisco. Comparing the Census Bureau’s 2011–2015 and 2016–2020 5 year American Community Survey reports, 117 of the 155 census tracts with estimates in both period, show an increase in average household income large enough that we can be confident it isn’t a product of survey error. The estimated change is small in the remaining 38 tracts relative to the survey’s margin of error. This means that the data can’t tell us whether incomes rose, fell, or held steady in those tracts. The largest confirmed increases are concentrated in and near the Downtown, which is an area that experienced substantially new housing and an influx of higher-earning residents. This corresponds to the trajectory of the tech boom, with a consistent increase in higher-earners moving to San Francisco in the 2010s. The increase is partly accounted for by who moved in, not only reflecting an increase for the people already living there. And because these figures are averages, a relatively small number of very high earners can pull a neighborhood’s number up. Rising averages are also consistent with the widening gap between rich and poor.

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

Grocery density helped most overall. In terms of transformation, the log of restaurant density was most effective. High-density land use was the most disappointing feature; It added almost nothing once logged restaurant density was in the model, likely because they both measure the same type of density, access, and walkability.
A one-percentage point increase in poverty rate is associated with a .42 (β̂) percentage point increase in predicted share of care free households, while holding all other variables constant.
In a tract where every other predictor is held at its average, at a 10% poverty rate, the model predicts 24.5% (ŷ) of households are carless.
The final residual map still shows clusters near Center City and West Philly. My model doesn’t account for transit access. It would be advantageous to add distance to the nearest SEPTA stop, bus stop density, or shared microbility hubs per square mile. It may be useful to add data on where concentrated areas of renters are, because they are less likely to own a car.
It doesn’t seem that the remaining error could be explained by noise. If it was, the largest misses would be in tracts with less reliable estimates. We see, however, that the biggest misses are in tracts with low CVs, meaning that the data should be relatively reliable. Only a few tracts have very high CVs, which could be explained by very few households that don’t have cars. Given this, it’s likely that the remaining error comes from variables the model doesn’t address.
